body:
Salt curing preserves meat mainly through osmosis. A high external concentration of sodium chloride draws water out of the meat tissue and out of the microbial cells in it. Microbes need water to grow, so pulling it away holds them back.

The useful measure here is water activity, written aw. It describes how much water is free and available, rather than the total water present. According to the USDA FSIS source, salt curing lowers water activity below 0.85, the threshold required for most bacterial growth. Salt also inhibits enzymatic actions inside cells.

Temperature matters because salt needs time to penetrate the meat. Until it does, the salt has not yet reached the inner tissue. The same source states that curing must be done at cool temperatures, typically below 4°C (40°F), to prevent pathogens from reproducing before salt penetration is complete.

This entry explains the mechanism only. It is not a curing recipe and gives no salt quantities, curing times or safety guarantees. The source excerpt does not address salt type, such as iodized versus non-iodized salt, so that question is left open here. Before curing meat to eat, follow a tested procedure from an authoritative food safety source.

sources.title: USDA FSIS — Food Safety of Cured Meats

summary: Salt cures meat mainly by osmosis: a high concentration of sodium chloride draws water out of meat tissue and microbial cells, lowering water activity below 0.85, the threshold most bacteria need to grow. Curing must stay cool, typically below 4°C (40°F), until the salt has penetrated.
title: Pull the water out with salt
